pos: n. (John Richardson, d. 1625, Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; English Richardson, son of Richard.
biblical_def: John Richardson sat in the First Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version, the group that rendered the books from the first of Chronicles through Ecclesiastes, and when its director Edward Lively died early in the work Richardson was among the men who carried it on. He was master of Peterhouse and then of Trinity, Regius Professor of Divinity, and he disputed with the Arminians at the Cambridge commencement. The portion his company handled is the most varied in the canon: royal chronicles, the book of Job, the whole Psalter, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes. Four very different kinds of Hebrew, one English voice. The Psalter in particular has been the prayer book of the English-speaking church for four centuries, and it came out of that room (Luk 24:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines psalter as the book of Psalms, and chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
PRO'VERB, n. A short sentence often repeated, expressing a well known truth or common fact, ascertained by experience or observation.
COMMENCE'MENT, n. The time when degrees are conferred in a college or university.

corruption_summary: His company rendered Chronicles through Ecclesiastes, and the Psalter came out of that room.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the Psalms from the rest of Scripture, so that they are read as devotional poetry detached from the covenant history that produced them. The First Cambridge Company handled both together, Chronicles and Psalms in the same commission, which is the order the canon itself keeps.

The principle to recover is that the Lord himself divided the Old Testament into law, prophets and psalms and said that all three speak of him. “all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me” (Luk 24:44). The psalms are given to the congregation for mutual instruction: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).

pos: n. (Francis Dillingham, d. 1625, Greek scholar of Christ's College and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Latin Franciscus, a Frank, a free man; English Dillingham, from a Bedfordshire place-name.
biblical_def: Francis Dillingham was a fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge, so good a Grecian that he was known in the university for disputing in Greek, and a member of the First Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. After the work he took the living of Wilden in Bedfordshire and wrote a long series of short practical books: a manual for the Christian householder, a disputation against Rome, guides to self-examination and to the right use of the sacraments. He gave the heavy end of his learning to the translation and the rest of his life to a village. That order is worth noticing. The gifts went first to the common text that everyone would use, and then to the people in front of him (Pro 25:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Grecian as one well versed in the Greek language, and manual as a small book, such as may be carried in the hand.
webster_full: GRE'CIAN, n. A native of Greece; also, one well versed in the Greek language.
MAN'UAL, n. A small book, such as may be carried in the hand, or conveniently handled.
HOUSE'HOLDER, n. The master or chief of a family; one who keeps house with his family.
DISPUTA'TION, n. A reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something, or on opposite sides.

And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: Greek good enough to dispute in, and the rest of his life in a Bedfordshire village.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern career logic that treats a village living after a national commission as a demotion. Dillingham appears to have seen it the other way. The translation was finished and would stand without him; the parish needed a man who could teach a household how to pray.

The principle to recover is that the same learning serves the text and the people, in that order and without conflict. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Pro 25:11). The double watch covers both duties: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1Ti 4:16). And the transmission is the point of the learning: “the same commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2).

pos: n. (Roger Andrewes, d. 1635, master of Jesus College and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Hrodgar, famous spear, through Roger; English Andrewes, from the Greek Andreas, manly.
biblical_def: Roger Andrewes was the younger brother of Lancelot Andrewes, who directed the First Westminster Company, and he sat himself in the First Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. He became master of Jesus College, archdeacon of Chichester, and a prebendary in his brother's cathedral at Winchester, and the preferments did not pass without comment among men who thought a bishop ought to be harder on his own family. The dictionary records the complaint and the work together. Nepotism is a real sin and advancement through a brother is a real temptation; and the man still sat for years in a committee rendering the Psalms into English. God is not obliged to use only those whose promotions were above criticism (Pro 16:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preferment as advancement to a higher office or dignity, and prebendary as a clergyman attached to a cathedral who enjoys a prebend.
webster_full: PREFER'MENT, n. Advancement to a higher office, dignity or station; promotion.
PREB'ENDARY, n. An ecclesiastic who enjoys a prebend; the stipendiary of a cathedral church.
ARCHDEA'CON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop, who has jurisdiction either over the whole or part of a diocese.
PATRONAGE, n. Special countenance or support; the right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice.

corruption_summary: Lancelot Andrewes's brother, promoted by him, and a translator of the Psalms.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of settling a historical question by a character verdict, as though a translator's career decided whether his rendering is right. It does not. Preferment through a brother is to be named as what it is, and the text he helped produce is to be judged by the Hebrew behind it.

The principle to recover is that God governs the steps of men who did not choose them well. “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). The standard for the servant remains unaltered by the manner of his appointment: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). And the final clause on any such work: “the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD” (Pro 16:1).

pos: n. (Robert Spalding, fl. 1605–1610, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Cambridge and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Hrodberht, bright in fame, through Robert; English Spalding, from the Lincolnshire town.
biblical_def: Robert Spalding was a fellow of St John's College, Cambridge, succeeded Edward Lively as Regius Professor of Hebrew when Lively died in 1605, and sat in the First Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. He was in turn succeeded in the chair by Geoffrey King, who also sat in a company. Three men in one Hebrew chair within a few years, all three translating: the universities had been quietly training up the exact skill the project would need, for reasons no one had planned. Hebrew had been taught in England for less than a century when the Authorized Version was made, and the work could not have been done a generation earlier. That is providence working through a curriculum (Ezr 7:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Hebrew as the language of the Hebrews, and chair as the office of a professor.
webster_full: HE'BREW, n. The language of the Hebrews; one of the Semitic languages, in which the Old Testament was written.
CHAIR, n. An official seat; hence, the office of a professor or of a presiding officer.
SUCCES'SOR, n. One that succeeds or follows; one who takes the place which another has left.
CUR'RICULUM, n. A course; particularly, a course of study in a university.

corruption_summary: Three men held one Cambridge Hebrew chair in a few years, and all three translated.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that the Authorized Version could have been produced at any time once the texts were available. It could not. It needed a generation of English Hebraists, and that generation existed because the universities had set up chairs and filled them for reasons of their own some decades earlier.

The principle to recover is that God prepares instruments before the work appears, and that a man preparing his heart to seek and to teach is doing the earlier half of a labour whose later half he cannot see. “Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezr 7:10). The direction is not the man's: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). And the skill itself is a gift: “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17).

pos: n. (Andrew Bing, 1574–1652, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Cambridge and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Greek Andreas, manly, through Andrew; English Bing, a family name of Norfolk.
biblical_def: Andrew Bing was a fellow of Peterhouse, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Cambridge after Geoffrey King, subdean and then archdeacon of York, and a member of the First Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. He outlived the version by forty-one years, long enough to see the civil war, the abolition of the episcopacy he served under, and the Westminster Assembly sitting in the building where kings were crowned. He was deprived of his preferments in 1642 and died in 1652. The dictionary records the length of his life for its own sake. A man who helps to render Scripture in his thirties may spend his seventies watching the world the version was made for come apart, and the version is still the version (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deprivation as the act of depriving or divesting of office, and endure as to last, to continue in the same state.
webster_full: DEPRIVA'TION, n. The act of depriving; a taking away; the act of divesting of office or dignity.
ENDURE', v.i. To last; to continue in the same state without perishing; to remain; to abide.
AR'CHDEACON, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary next in rank below a bishop.
SEQUESTRA'TION, n. The act of taking property from the owner for a time, till the rents and profits satisfy a demand.

corruption_summary: He outlived the version by forty-one years and saw the world it was made for come apart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of Scripture's authority with the stability of the order that happens to publish it. Bing's England collapsed. The bishops were abolished, the king was executed, his own livings were sequestered, and the Bible he had helped translate was carried straight through all of it by the men on the other side of the war.

The principle to recover is that the word outlasts every institution that handles it. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Peter quotes the same prophet and applies it to the gospel just preached: “But the word of the Lord endureth for ever” (1Pe 1:25). And the smallest part of it is secured: “one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18).

pos: n. (John Duport, d. 1617, master of Jesus College and director of the Second Cambridge Company)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; French Duport, of the gate or harbour, a Huguenot family name.
biblical_def: John Duport was master of Jesus College, Cambridge, four times vice-chancellor of the university, and he directed the Second Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version, the company assigned the books of the Apocrypha. That assignment is worth stating carefully. The translators rendered those books because the version was to be the Bible of a national church whose lectionary read them, and they placed them between the Testaments, not within either; the Thirty-nine Articles and the later Reformed confessions alike deny them canonical authority. The dictionary holds the sixty-six-book canon without reservation. Duport's company did careful work on books the church reads for example of life and instruction of manners and does not use to establish any doctrine (Deu 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apocrypha as books whose authors are not known and which are not admitted to be inspired, and canon as a law or rule, the genuine books of Scripture.
webster_full: APOC'RYPHA, n. Books whose authors are not known; books not admitted to be inspired, and therefore not received into the canon of Scripture.
CAN'ON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline; the genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon.
LEC'TIONARY, n. The Romish service book, containing portions of Scripture; a book of lessons appointed to be read.
APPEN'DIX, n. Something appended or added; a supplement or short treatise added to a book.

corruption_summary: His company rendered the Apocrypha, and placed it between the Testaments and not within them.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the Roman error directly. The Council of Trent in 1546 declared the apocryphal books canonical and anathematized those who did not receive them, which added to the canon the Jewish church had kept and from which our Lord quoted, and which supplied the proof texts for purgatory and for prayer for the dead. The Reformed churches did not burn the books; they printed them where they belong, outside the canon, and the Authorized Version of 1611 did exactly that.

The principle to recover is that the canon is closed and that adding to it is forbidden in the same terms as taking from it. “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2). The last book of the canon repeats the prohibition for itself: “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18). And the Lord's own threefold division of the Old Testament has no fourth part: “in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms” (Luk 24:44).

pos: n. (William Branthwaite, 1563–1619, master of Gonville and Caius and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; English Branthwaite, from a Cumberland place-name.
biblical_def: William Branthwaite was a fellow of Emmanuel College in its first Puritan generation, master of Gonville and Caius, and a member of the Second Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. Emmanuel had been founded in 1584 expressly to train preachers, and it bred the men who would later sit in the Westminster Assembly and settle New England; Branthwaite is the link between that house and the version. He left his books to his college. The dictionary notes the combination that is easy to miss at this distance: a convinced Puritan, working under a king who disliked Puritans, on a Bible that both would use, and doing it without a rendering that favours either party (1Co 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Puritan as one who affected extraordinary purity in religious worship, and bequeath as to give or leave by will.
webster_full: PU'RITAN, n. One who affected or professed extraordinary purity in the forms of religious worship, and objected to the ceremonies retained in the church.
BEQUEATH', v.t. To give or leave by will; to devise some species of property by testament.
COL'LEGE, n. In a general sense, a collection or assemblage; a society of men, set apart for learning or religion.
IM'PARTIAL, a. Not partial; not biased in favor of one party more than another; indifferent.

corruption_summary: An Emmanuel Puritan rendering Scripture under a king who disliked Puritans.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion that every translation encodes its committee's party. The Authorized Version is the hardest case for that theory. It was produced by bishops and Puritans sitting in the same rooms under rules that forbade marginal notes of interpretation, and the result served both sides and then outlived both.

The principle to recover is that the words are the Holy Ghost's and the translator's business is to carry them, not to steer them. “Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth” (1Co 2:13). The purity claimed is the text's: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6). And Paul's own standard forbids selection: “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27).

pos: n. (Jeremiah Radcliffe, d. 1612, vice-master of Trinity College and translator of the Authorized Version)
etymology: Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the LORD exalts, through Jeremiah; English Radcliffe, from a northern place-name meaning red cliff.
biblical_def: Jeremiah Radcliffe was vice-master of Trinity College, Cambridge, a doctor of divinity, and a member of the Second Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version. He died in 1612, within a year of the version's appearing, and almost nothing of him survives beyond the college records and the list of translators. The dictionary keeps him for the same reason it keeps Geoffrey King and Gaspard Laurent. A great work has a great many hands in it whose owners are invisible, and the believer's reward is not administered by posterity. The accounting is held elsewhere and the standard is one word (1Co 4:2).

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that an unrecorded labour was a small one. Fifty men produced the Authorized Version and perhaps a dozen are remembered; the rest did the same hours over the same Hebrew and Greek, and the pages are not divided by reputation.

The principle to recover is that the reward of hidden work is promised and is not paid by historians. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). The Lord states the arrangement plainly: “That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:4). And the publishing of the word is credited to a company, not a man: “great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11).

pos: n. (John Bois, 1561–1644, translator of the Authorized Version and one of its final revisers)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; French Bois, a wood, a Huguenot family name.
biblical_def: John Bois read Hebrew at five, taught by his father, and was reading the Greek New Testament through at six in the morning in the Cambridge university library as an undergraduate. He sat in the Second Cambridge Company for the Authorized Version, and then was one of the twelve men chosen from the six companies for the final revision at Stationers' Hall, nine months of reading the whole version aloud and settling every disputed rendering. He took notes, and his notes are the only record anybody kept of that room. Afterwards he spent forty years as rector of Boxworth and died at eighty-three. He is the nearest thing the Authorized Version has to an eyewitness, and what his notes show is argument, evidence, and men changing their minds (Pro 15:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revise as to review and correct, and collate as to compare, to examine two things of the same kind.
webster_full: REVI'SE, v.t. To review; to re-examine; to look over with care for correction; as, to revise a writing.
COLLA'TE, v.t. To compare; to examine two or more things of the same kind, as writings or copies, to ascertain their agreement.
AMANUEN'SIS, n. A person who writes what another dictates; one who copies what another has written.
REN'DERING, n. A version; a translation; the act of giving the sense of one language in another.

Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
corruption_summary: The only man who took notes at the final revision, and the Authorized Version's one eyewitness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the romantic account of the Authorized Version as a work of sudden inspiration, which its own records contradict. Bois's notes show a committee reading aloud, weighing the Greek Fathers, comparing earlier English versions, arguing about particles, and sometimes deciding against the man who had done the first draft.

The principle to recover is that counsel is a means God ordains and that haste in judgment is a shame. “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). An answer in its due season is itself a good: “A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it” (Pro 15:23). And the opposite is named: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13).

pos: n. (William Barlow, d. 1613, bishop of Lincoln and director of the Second Westminster Company)
etymology: Germanic Wilhelm, resolute protector; English Barlow, from a Lancashire or Derbyshire place-name.
biblical_def: William Barlow was dean of Chester, bishop of Rochester and then of Lincoln, and he directed the Second Westminster Company for the Authorized Version, which rendered the Epistles from Romans to Jude. He had been present at the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 and wrote the official account of it, the account that records the Puritan John Rainolds proposing a new translation and the king agreeing. Barlow's report is partisan against the Puritan side, and the dictionary says so; it is also the only full record of the meeting at which the version was commissioned. His company's portion contains the doctrine of justification, the whole argument of Romans, and the pastoral epistles (Rom 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines epistle as a writing communicated from one person to another, and conference as a meeting for consultation or discussion.
webster_full: EPIS'TLE, n. A writing, directed or sent, communicating intelligence to a distant person; a letter.
CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of two or more persons for consulting on some serious matter; a formal discourse or oral discussion.
PAR'TIAL, a. Inclined to favor one party in a cause, or one side of a question, more than the other.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director.
scriptures: Rom 3:2
Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
corruption_summary: His company rendered Romans to Jude, and he wrote the one record of Hampton Court.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the uncritical use of a partisan source because it is the only source. Barlow wrote the Hampton Court account to put the Puritans in the worst light available, and historians have had to read it against the grain for four centuries. The detail he had no motive to invent, Rainolds asking for a new translation and the king consenting, is therefore the firmest fact in it.

The principle to recover is that God committed his oracles to the church and uses interested men to transmit them, and that the whole counsel is to be declared whatever a party would prefer. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2). Paul's standard admits no editing: “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). And all of it is profitable, including the parts a translator's party dislikes: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16).
